questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer:
Finding off campus housing was an incredibly difficult task. Me and my friend from UCPH searched for housing together when we arrived in Sydney. Thus, I can only describe the difficulty of finding housing for two or more people. We began our search in different Facebook groups and on
Flatmates.com.au
where we came across a lot of poor quality rooms and several rental agreements with quite burdensome (probably even illegal) terms and conditions. We then switched our search platform to
Realestate.com.au
after being told that it was THE platform in Sydney. We went to several inspections before we were offered the flat we ended up living in.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer: If you choose to live off campus, you should definitely find out whether other students from your home uni, who has been on an exchange the previous semester, are able to pass on their accomodation on to you. Otherwise, you must be prepared for the Sydney housing market which is quite harsh compared to the Copenhagen market. When you find a flat, that you're interested in, you must attend an inspection of the property which is held at a specific time and date. The inspection is attended by anyone who's interested so the amount of visitors typically range from 0 to 30. If you're still interested in the property after the inspection, the landlord or the landlord's agent will write down your information. If the landlord offers the property to you, both the bond and 1-2 weeks rent must be paid to the landlord or the landlord's agent before you receive a filled out rental agreement. Naturally, we we're quite reluctant of paying money before receiving the agreement and, consequently, we lost a few offers. However, this practice was confimed to us by several different real estate agents. Furthermore, the bond is normally paid to a government controlled platform which reduces the risk of being scammed.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I was very satisfied with my off campus apartment as it was located in the a central suburb and was in a mint condition. However, choosing on campus housing (Queen Mary Building) would have been a better solution both economically and socially.

questions.answer: The registration process took a lot of time but it was fairly easy as USYD's exchange counselor provided a lot of guidance and sent several reminders regarding deadlines etc.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: USYD's exchange counselor, Jane Andrews, was able to answer all questions regarding registration.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: I applied for eight different classes. I was eventually offered five of them.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Begin the registration proces as soon as possible as it takes a lot of time.

questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Did you take BA or MA courses at your host university? *
questions.answer: MA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: My four courses were exciting but quite difficult. The coursework was quite heavy and it took a lot of effort to understand the basics of Common Law. Furthermore, two of my courses (Corporations Law and Evidence Law) were mandatory for domestic postgraduate students and, therefore, the courses built upon the knowledge that the domestic students had obtained in previous courses.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: It was more or less the same. USYD had, however, introduced a 70 % attendance requirement.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer: International Commercial Arbitration. IP: Copyright and Designs. Corporations Law. Evidence Law.

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: International Commercial Arbitration. Professor Chester Brown is a top-level lecturer and he has a lot of practical experience with arbitration. Furthermore, the relevance of the course is not limited to Australia.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: I wasn't engaged in any clubs. I, however, bought access to the campus fitness gym which included access to a climbing wall and a swimming pool.

questions.question: What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: USU (University of Sydney Union) hosts a lot of events during the semester. Everything from concerts to food markets.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: Attend as many social events on campus as possible as it is a great opportunity to get to know your peers.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: Explore Sydney. For longer trips, go to The Blue Mountains and Royal National Park.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: Fairly easy. Despite the location on the other side of the planet, Sydney seems very European.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: Reach out to the local students during class.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: Be prepared for a lot of small talk due to the common "How are you doing?" every time you meet someone.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: People in Sydney are very friendly and open-minded.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer:
Explore Australia as much as possible both before, during and after the semester. 
Save up a lot of money - you will undoubtedly spend a lot of money. 
Be completely sure before accepting the courses that you're offered - it will be close to impossible to change them after the semester has started.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: Avoid courses that are mandatory for domestic students. You will lack a lot of the prerequisites needed (especially the understanding of Common Law).

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: Living in Sydney for almost five months is one of the greatest experiences I've ever had.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: The coursework
